No one may publish

NOTE:

This judgment is intended to comply with the restriction so that it may be
published.

Decision of the

Honourable Judge
J.R. Shaw

NOTE:
This judgment was delivered orally
in Court. It has since been edited for the purposes of publication. Headings
were added and minor grammatical changes were made. As well, a sentence in
paragraph 139 was added after the judgment was delivered in Court.

[
1
]

This hearing heard the application by the
Director of Child and Family Services (the “Director”) for a Permanent
Guardianship Order (PGO) under the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act

(“
CYFEA
”) and three private guardianship applications under the
Family
Law Act
(“
FLA
”) by the paternal grandparents, DM and MM (hereinafter
collectively “M’s” or the “M’s”), plus their eldest son GM, who would be the
paternal uncle to the three children. The three children, GBM, MJM, and TEM,
who are nine, seven and three years old respectively.

[
2
]

This was a longer than usual hearing, truncated,
commencing in March and concluding in May of 2014, with an additional eight
pre-hearing days for the herculean task performed by a senior Judge of this
division, in overseeing the difficult pre-hearing case management that was
required. What was more unusual, neither of the parents, the mother MMF (aka MF)
or the father NM, both guardians of the children, testified. The father did not
attend the hearing at all, although notified; he last attended these
proceedings up to December 6, 2012, with counsel and then appeared to abandon
all interest in his three children.  The mother attended eleven of the sixteen
hearing days and although time was reserved for her testimony, she declined
through her counsel.

[
3
]

GM, the paternal uncle to the three children,
was the only guardianship applicant to testify. The paternal grandparents chose
not to testify. All three M family guardianship applicants represented
themselves. All three family guardianship applicants were given a copy of
Exhibit #5, “The Unrepresented Respondent in Family and Child Welfare Matters”,
appended to this decision. Additionally, the M’s were read a brief summary of
the rule in
Browne v. Dunn
(1893) 6 R, 67, H.L.:

“If
counsel intends to impeach the credibility of a witness by calling independent
evidence later the witness must first be confronted with the intended evidence
during cross examination to give the witness a fair opportunity to explain or
respond while on the witness stand.”

[
4
]

GM was not present for that reading; he did not
attend for twelve of the sixteen hearing days.

[
5
]

The Court proceeded as if this was a
K.V.W.
v. Alberta Director of Child Welfare

2006 ABCA 404
situation, where the
guardianship applications are to be decided prior to the PGO. With the
agreement of all parties, all evidence was to be heard first. As a courtesy to
the self-represented M’s, DM, MM and GM, the Director opened with their case
and the M’s were permitted to cross-examine last, giving them an opportunity to
observe how the lawyers conducted cross-examination. The M’s were permitted to
argue last, thereby giving them an opportunity to hear all prior submissions:
three submissions from the three lawyers representing the Director, the mother,
MMF aka F, and the lawyer representing the children.

[
6
]

The mother and guardian, MMF, was not consenting
to the guardianship applications of any party and certainly not by any member
of the M family. The father and guardian, NM, evidently signed a consent in
Texas on January 2, 2012, authorizing his mother, father and brother to seek
guardianship of the three children and another handwritten “consent” of
questionable authenticity dated July 3, 2013. Mr. NM did not testify at the
trial or confirm his consent. The Court heard conflicting evidence from child
care professionals that NM, the father, would not sign or give his consent to
any therapist working with his children so that information could be shared
with the paternal grandparents, DM and MM, nor could they be involved in any
therapy with the children as non-guardians. In the end, although the two
guardians and biological parents remain bitterly divided, neither one would
permit information to be shared with or therapeutic access to DM and MM and, by
extension, GM.

[
7
]

The father, NM, is in the unenviable position of
being on bail facing charges of sexual assault and sexual interference while he
had access to these three children, who are the subject of this hearing.
Evidently, the criminal trial will be heard in December of 2014. This Court
finds that he is aware of these proceedings, and he has not been permitted
access since the children’s apprehension on May 2, 2012. He has abandoned these
children – he still has a parenting application ongoing, which neither the father
nor agent on his behalf attended to speak to.

[
8
]

The mother, through her counsel, in final and
emotional submissions, acknowledged that at this point in time, she is not in a
position to parent the children – a very mature observation – certainly
supported by the evidence heard and by her own expert’s report, Dr. Tittemore
[Exhibit #31]. I shall refer later to disclosures in exhibits relating to the
mother’s involvement and apparent knowledge surrounding the sexual, emotional
and physical abuse suffered by these three children.

[
9
]

This Court has in the intervening time read,
re-read, viewed and reviewed, all evidence heard, viewed and entered at the
hearing. The cart full of evidence has left an impression in my chambers carpet
and in my mind. I cannot repeat all of the evidence without writing a decision
as long as Tolstoy’s “War and Peace” and while the title is appropriate for
this case, given the enmity and “scorched earth” approach pursued by some of
the litigants, I shall try to write short. Simply because not every “jot and
tittle” of evidence has been mentioned does not mean that it has been
overlooked.

[
10
]

On the first day of this hearing, the Alberta
Court of Appeal rendered its decision on an appeal by DM and MM from an interim
order by the case managing Judge, reported as
D.M. and M.M v. Alberta
(
Child,
Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director)

2014 ABCA 92
. It is a brief
decision, appended to the back of this decision.

[
11
]

This Court has heard disturbing evidence, reviewed
below, with some disquieting religious overtones. The future litigation of this
file appears to be predictably ongoing, which would not be in the best
interests of these three children, caught in a classic Shakespearean “Montague
and Capulet” scenario where “all are punished”.

[
12
]

The M family first came to the attention of
Child Welfare in October of 2010, then only two children at that time, due to
allegations of neglect, verbal abuse and illegal drug use. At that time, DM and
MM, as paternal grandparents, were seen as a safe haven, a protective factor,
for the children and no further intervention was taken. The Court heard
evidence from GM that as far back as 2008, the M family, at least DM and MM,
had planned to have the children raised by their paternal uncle, GM.

[
13
]

MMF was 15 years of age when she met the father,
NM, then 24 years old, in Saskatoon. Pregnant by the age of 16 years with the
first of her three children, the couple moved to Calgary where they were
generally supported by DM and MM. Domestic disharmony continued to grow and the
Court is satisfied that DM and MM took a commanding role in raising and
supporting their now five dependents: the two parents, NM and MMF, and the
three children.

[
14
]

Mr. TJ testified that he is a neighbour to the M’s
and how on the evening of December 26, 2011, MMF came to their door upset and
crying with the three children asking for help – “she was tired of the abuse”
and wanted the police called. When the police and DM arrived, they instructed DM
not to contact MMF or the J family and permitted Mr. TJ, a City of Calgary
Transit Peace Officer, to take MMF with the three children to a women’s
shelter. For their Good Samaritan efforts, Mrs. J, with her children, was
approached by MM in a store and yelled at, whereas Mr. DM complained to Mr. TJ’s
City employer after Mr. TJ made a court appearance wearing his City Transit
Peace Officer uniform.

[
15
]

By January 3, 2012, the mother, MMF, had
returned to her parents’ home with the three children in S[...], Saskatchewan
and had been there several days when Alberta Child and Family Services, at the
insistent urging of DM and MM, and possibly NM, made a referral to Saskatchewan
Child Welfare. DM was frantically contacting managers over this Christmas
holiday, telling anyone who would listen that the children were unsafe with
their mother and maternal grandparents; that the children should be returned to
them; that the mother, a legal guardian, should never have been permitted to
leave. After three days, by January 6, 2012, Ms. Amber Potts, team leader here
in Calgary with Child and Family Services, was able to speak with the mother, MMF,
and the maternal Grandmother, EL. Saskatchewan Child Welfare authorities had
already made a home visit. Not satisfied, DM accompanied his son, NM, to this
Courthouse on January 6, 2012, and obtained an Ex Parte Parenting Order from a
Judge in this Division, when they knew where the children were. DM travelled to
Saskatchewan on January 7, 2012, to meet with the RCMP and apprehend the three
children from their mother and maternal grandparents.

[
16
]

This is the crux of this hearing. The children,
after returning from the approximate ten days in Saskatchewan and seven days
after in Texas where the two eldest were taken to visit Uncle GM and their
father, NM, allegedly made disclosures of abuse and sexual abuse while in S[...],
Saskatchewan to all adult members of the M family.

[
17
]

These allegations of abuse were recanted by the
children, the police and social services investigated. The maternal grandmother
passed a polygraph and by January 26, 2012, Child and Family Services advised
the father, NM, that the children were being coached and influenced; that the
children’s stories differed from the version proffered by DM, MM and NM. This
had become an unpleasant custody dispute, with unsubstantiated allegations of
abuse, emotional, physical and sexual.

[
18
]

The applicants for private guardianship, DM, MM
and GM, all maintain that the three children were abused during the 10 days in S[...],
Saskatchewan, with and by the maternal side of the family. They are
irresolvably entrenched in their position that the Director was negligent in
permitting the mother to travel with the three children to Saskatchewan and
should have done more to procure their return. The Court finds on the evidence
heard and the Alberta Court of Appeal decision
D.M. and M.M. v. Alberta
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director
,
2014 ABCA 92
that DM and
MM were extremely agitated that other cousins and family members should be
permitted post-apprehension access with their grandchildren when they were not.

[
19
]

The M’s entrenched position is difficult to
comprehend when after the May 2, 2012, apprehension, the compelling and
detailed evidence began to emerge that both the biological parents were
involved in some sexual abuse with the daughter MJM, and the father further
abusing GBM and TEM. The M grandparents maintain that the abuse occurred; just
the name of the perpetrator is at issue. On that point, the Court agrees with
them.

The Evidence of Amber Potts

[
20
]

Amber Potts was a social worker and team leader
at the time the mother, MMF, took the three children to S[...], Saskatchewan.
She testified about the efforts Child and Family Services made pre and post
Saskatchewan. Two social workers interviewed MMF at the Women’s Shelter on
December 27, 201l, and were told of the father, NM, sexually assaulting the
mother, MMF, throwing a tantrum, threatening to slit her throat, smashing the Christmas
tree ornaments and breaking the children’s Christmas gifts. Ms. Potts was behind
the one-way glass when GBM and MJM were interviewed January 24, 2012, by JICAT,
a joint investigation child abuse team, after complaints by DM and NM - the
last complaint was that spiders and snakes had been thrown at MJM (in
Saskatchewan in January).

[
21
]

GBM revealed abuse disclosures such as drinking
pee from the toilet, eating poo and being hit with a stick by P, his maternal
grandfather. MJM commenced with similar stories – she was sad, she had been
told that she did not have a mom anymore. Ms. Potts observed and heard MJM say,
“Do you want to know the real truth? Nothing happened to us. P [the maternal
grandfather] did nothing”. The JICAT team felt that MJM was telling the real
truth – that nothing bad had happened. Still, there was a concern – both GBM
and MJM reported that they no longer had a mommy, a very cruel thing to tell a
child during a custody dispute. Other concerns remained; Child and Family
Services could not just drop this file and leave the three children in their
father’s custody. There were still lingering concerns around the sexual abuse
allegations, the emotional injury to the children access driven and the
domestic violence that they witnessed, including arguments between DM, MM and NM.
Both parents, NM and MMF had mental health issues, while the maternal
grandfather had alcohol-use concerns. Then there was the police report that NM
had allegedly tried to touch the private parts of the 12-year-old daughter of a
family friend.

[
22
]

Ms. Potts was involved in the May 2, 2012,
apprehension and was dismayed to learn that DM and MM did not listen to the
instructions to not leave the children with NM. When she arrived to apprehend,
only the youngest TEM was with her grandparents, the other two siblings were at
NM’s house with their father and GM.

The Evidence of Ashley Mahmood

[
23
]

This caseworker followed after Ms. Potts on the
file and worked with the family. She testified that the Director still wished
to pursue any sexual abuse allegations and how the custodial guardian, NM,
would not bring his children in for an exam in January even though he was not
working and refused to let his parents, DM and MM, bring them. As such, the
child abuse physical did not take place until May 2, 2012, with the resulting
evidential finding of full transection of MJM’s hymen and the immediate
apprehension. Ms. Mahmood is able to testify about MJM’s May 24, 2012, Calgary
Police Service interview with Detective Teresa Swindell, Sex Crimes [Exhibit
#3, Binder 2A, Tab #11] . MJM stated that her Dad makes her suck on his penis
and it makes her puke, be sick – it happened more than once. MJM identified her
father by pointing to a collage of family photographs and said “my dad, NM”, as
the person who did this to her. Further disclosure revealed how her father
would make her squat on the toilet and watch her pee, then put his penis in her
vagina – it hurt; she cried.

[
24
]

GBM was also interviewed by Detective Swindell
with Ms. Mahmood taking notes [Exhibit #3, Binder 2A, Tab #12]. GBM was very
distraught and cried; he did not want to talk about MJM’s secret. He did state
that “my grandpa told me not to tell the truth – not to talk to you – to sit
and cry”. GBM was sad and upset when this same grandpa, DM, told him that he
did not like his mom and kicked her out of the house. This little boy missed
his mother and feared that she would not come back. He also expressed concern
for his two siblings during this interview.

[
25
]

Ms. Mahmood also tried to work with the mother, MMF,
and her reported new husband, AF, accessing services. The marriage ruse was
untruthful and the mother, MMF, by the end of July 2012, had moved in with
another man called N.

[
26
]

Ms. Mahmood testified about the lengths that the
Director went to in order to ensure that the children retained some contact
with the Jewish part of their heritage. This included liaising with Jewish
Family Services and the M’s, time and respite weekends with a Calgary Jewish
family and enrollment in the Calgary Jewish Academy, for the eligible children,
at a cost of $9,000.00 a year per child, paid for by the Director (taxpayer).
This Court remarked how many a mother in N.E. Calgary might be relieved if her
children, while apprehended, were sent to private schools, paid for by the
taxpayer. One difficulty with the Calgary Jewish Academy was that it did not
want the children enrolled if it meant dealing with DM and MM, as they were
deemed too difficult to work with and had accused people at the school of being
anti-Semitic. This is a constant and recurring theme with DM and MM, being
perceived as too difficult to work with and accusing others of being
anti-Semitic. The Director persisted and the Calgary Jewish Academy agreed to
enroll the children so long as contact would be primarily through the foster
parents and not DM and MM.

[
27
]

Three unsuccessful concurrent plans were
prepared to try to reunite this fractured family. Ms. Mahmood asked to be
relieved from this file and shortly after, some unpleasant communications from
the father, NM [Exhibit #2, Binder 2, Tab 24], were received where she was
called a Muslim terrorist, among other vile unpleasantries. Her contact, as
well as other’s, with NM was generally described as not pleasant.

[
28
]

Ongoing concerns whether or not DM, MM or GM
could protect the children from their father, NM, remain from Ms. Mahmood’s
carriage of the file to the present day. MJM had stated to her that she wanted
to see her grandparents, but only if her dad is in jail, and she is safe.
During her time with this file, DM and MM continued to disregard boundaries set
up to protect the children. A letter had to be handed to them again setting out
the boundaries. Access between the three children and their paternal
grandparents was eventually terminated because of repeated and significant
breaches.

[
29
]

During Ms. Mahmood’s tenure, the M grandparents
had more meetings, sometimes weekly, with Child and Family Services than given
to any other non-guardian grandparents.

The Evidence of Andrea Silverstone

[
30
]

Ms. Silverstone is a domestic violence and child
abuse specialist with Jewish Family Services. She was liaison between Child
Welfare and DM and MM since May 2012. They intervene when Jewish children are
in care of the Director. Her evidence was, in response to another complaint by DM
that the Director was behaving in an anti-Semitic fashion, was that the
Director was doing what it could to navigate a very complex issue. She
testified that people generally have conflict with the M’s and that the M’s
called Jewish Family Services anti-Semitic. In response to DM’s cross-examination,
she replied that “you might feel that they [meaning the Director] are anti-M,
but they are not anti-Semitic”.

[
31
]

Ms. Silverstone testified how the current foster
parents, a Christian pastor and his wife, have been very cooperative with
Jewish Family Services, as had the Provincial case and social workers – really
all parties, except DM and MM.

[
32
]

Ms. Silverstone also testified about an email
letter sent by DM [Exhibit #11] to “undisclosed recipients” related to the
arrests of the maternal grandfather for the sexual abuse of the M
grandchildren. She knew of the three parents who had received this letter, one
of whom forwarded it to her, apparently traumatised. The Court heard no
evidence on what response, if any, the children received at school. In the
Court’s opinion, Mr. DM shows an appalling lack of insight, certainly no
respect, by publishing the confidential disclosures of his own grandchildren.
For what purpose you may ask; a narcissistic delight in being able to say, “I
told you so”? Charges were later dropped against the maternal grandfather. Ms.
Silverstone felt that these, now identified M children, would be stigmatised in
the Jewish community as victims of sexual or domestic violence.

[
33
]

Ms. Silverstone had a ready answer for the
problems that the three children would face growing up, “let them be raised
Jewish”. She testified that Ms. MM was not Jewish, although married to DM, and
that the M’s were currently attending church, possibly not because of any
religious desire, but that they had discovered the identity of the foster
parents and were attending his church where he was the Pastor.

[
34
]

The Court heard evidence from other sources
dealing with “the religious issue” and finds that the mother, MMF, and the
maternal grandparents are Christian. Ms. MM is a born again Christian from
Mennonite stock in Ontario. Mr. DM is Jewish from Poland. The father, NM, is
evidently Jewish, whether practising or not, we do not know. Neither parent and
guardians, MMF or NM, were married in a civil or religious ceremony. None of
the legal guardians have affirmed any dedication to raise these three children
in either the Christian or Jewish religion. We know the children were about to
celebrate Christmas in 2011 before their mother moved them to Saskatchewan. The
children have equal contributors to their DNA, as well as equal heritage or
cultural contributors. It would be a gross oversimplification to say that they
are half this, or half that – it is one of the responsibilities or obligations
that guardians are entrusted with, and this Court is relieved at not having to
make a ruling on race or culture.

[
35
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has written on those
issues, recently in
Van de Perre v. Edwards
, [2001] SCR 1014, and
specifically at paragraphs 36 through to 42, under “
II The Importance of
Race in the Custody Determination of a Child of Mixed Racial Heritage
”. Our
Supreme Court recognises the importance of a child’s “cultural identity” and
how the “significance of evidence relating to race in any given custody case
must be carefully considered by the trial judge” [para. 40].

[
36
]

It (race) is but one factor and must be
considered pragmatically [para. 38]. The paramount concern, the best interests
of the children, remains and has not been displaced.

[
37
]

The Supreme Court dealt with the aboriginal
cultural heritage in an earlier decision,
Racine v. Woods
1983 CanLII 27 (SCC)
, [1983] 2 SCR
173. Madame Justice Wilson opened her judgment with:

“This
appeal emphasizes once more, this time in an interracial context that the law
no longer treats children as the property of those who gave them birth but
focuses on what is in their best interests”.

[
38
]

Without appearing too prolix, the following
observation by Justice Wilson is worth repeating and reminding myself at page
185:

“Be that as it
may, I do not think a finding of abandonment was necessary to the judge’s
decision. I think the statue is clear and that s. 103(2) dispenses with
parental consent in the case of a
de facto
adoption. This does not mean,
of course, that the child’s tie with its natural parent is irrelevant in making
of an order under the section. It is obviously very relevant in a determination
as to what is in the child’s best interests. But it is the parental tie as a
meaningful and positive force in the life of the child and not in the life of
the parent that the court has to be concerned about. As has been emphasized
many times in custody cases, a child is not a chattel in which its parents have
a proprietary interest; it is a human being to whom they owe serious
obligations. In giving the court power to dispense with the consent of the
parent on a
de facto
adoption the legislature has recognized an aspect
of the human condition – that our own self interest sometimes clouds our
perception of what is best for those for whom we are responsible. It takes a
very high degree of selflessness and maturity – for most of us probably an
unattainable degree – for a parent to acknowledge that it might be better for
his or her child to be brought up by someone else. The legislature in its
wisdom has protected the child against this human frailty in a case where
others have stepped into the breach and provided a happy and secure home for
the child for a minimum period of three consecutive years. In effect, these
persons have assumed the obligations of the natural parents and taken their
place. The natural parents’ consent in these circumstances is no longer
required.”

The Evidence of Dr. Jennifer Reid MacPherson.

[
39
]

This witness was qualified as an expert in
pediatrics with expertise in medical examination of child sexual abuse. She
examined the three M children on May 2, 2012, with their parents present. The
child, TEM, was 13 months at the time. No concerns were shown, no evidence of
abuse. Dr. MacPerson had reviewed an earlier report by Dr. Dowling, who had
examined both TEM and MJM after their return from Saskatchewan, and in cross
examination told DM that Dr. Dowling didn’t believe there had been a sexual
assault (in his report).

[
40
]

GBM was examined, while both his parents were
outside the examining room, and again no findings of any concern – no evidence
of sexual abuse. She was aware at the time that one of the parents was alleged
to be a perpetrator of sexual abuse.

[
41
]

MJM was almost five years old, one month away,
when she was examined, with both her parents there on opposite sides of a
pulled curtain. Dr. MacPherson found a complete transection of MJM’s hymen,
with the edges quite rounded and wide at the 6 o’clock location. The trauma at
this location was bad, “a full tear – no question”. In her opinion, this was
probably older than a week, but not within the last few days. Dr. MacPherson
could not determine if what was inserted could have been a finger or a penis.

[
42
]

Dr. MacPherson observed NM staring at the
computer screen with a large image of MJM’s genitalia. In her experience,
fathers did not stare at images of their daughter’s vagina. When she moved the
computer screen, NM would move his head to follow the image. The father, NM,
then had to be told to go to the other side of the curtain so he could not see any
more images. Dr. MacPherson caught him peeking around the curtain. She
testified that she “felt disturbed and alarmed by the whole process of MJM’s
father with his intense, fixed stare at the computer screen”.

The Evidence of Donkia Collins

[
43
]

This veteran caseworker has been on this file
since July 2013, when both parents were charged criminally with abusing the
children, and neither had access as a term of their bail release. Criminal
charges were withdrawn against the mother, MMF, on October 10, 2013, and her
access was reinstated. The mother was attending parenting classes, had
completed a parenting assessment, was evidently taking courses regarding sexual
abuse and was tending to her epilepsy medications (grand mal seizures), still
had work to do with her mental health counselling and generally family of origin
issues. The father, NM, by contrast was, and remains, non-cooperative, did not
complete the parenting assessment or the court ordered risk to sexual abuse
assessment.

[
44
]

She was aware of the 12 Recommendations for DM
and MM contained in Dr. During’s assessment and how the therapy set up for the M
grandparents was vital [Binder 1, Tab #3, p.24]. At the request of the M’s, the
Director agreed to pay for independent therapy with two senior psychologists,
Ms. Hazelwood and Chris Berry. Neither Mr. or Mrs. M attended for the scheduled
sessions. Then DM called after the second missed appointment to say that they
would not be attending, that their lawyer said it was not in their best
interests at this time. There was no request by either M for different
psychologists. This was perceived by Ms. Collins as another example of DM and MM’s
refusal to work collaboratively with the Director.

[
45
]

MM’s access to the children was reinstated for
June and July of 2013. The children had to be moved to a different foster home
because DM and MM found out their identity. Now the children were all together
in the same foster home for the first time. They were quietly placed with the C’s;
Mr. BC was a Pastor. Within weeks of this Child Welfare confidential placement,
however, the M’s, DM and MM, had ferreted out their identities, address and had
started attending their Church; MM, with her strong voice, even sang in the
choir. This was done to try to see their three grandchildren.

[
46
]

This Court has never read the identities of
foster parents in any report; their confidentiality is always protected. The M’s,
DM and MM, were able to breach that confidential shield. Another disturbing
piece of evidence repeated throughout this hearing came from witnesses who felt
their emails were compromised or breached. DM particularly would show up at the
foster home, the foster father’s office, the Church, the supermarket, the
swimming pool, several times when somehow he knew when the children would be
taking swim lessons. DM would telephone and email the foster home, all contrary
to explicit and written instructions from the Director’s workers not to [Binder
2, Tab #84].

[
47
]

On August 22, 2013, DM showed up at Jewish Camp,
when he was not supposed to know MJM was there. He approached her and told her
to keep it a secret. The Court finds that this is an egregious lack of insight
on DM’s part to tell a young six-year-old girl, who everyone acknowledged was a
victim of sexual abuse (only the name of the perpetrator is an issue), to keep
a secret.

[
48
]

The M’s, DM and MM, were called to the
Director’s Hunterhorn office to discuss consequences for the continuous breaches
on September 5, 2013. Ms. Chasity Goett was the supervisor, arriving late with
youngest child, who had been taken to synagogue. DM was overheard several times
saying to GBM “when you come home with us”. MM was whispering to MJM who stood
up and yelled, “No, P [her maternal grandfather] did not hurt me – he did not
hurt me”. MM said loudly, “She has been telling lies for over a year now”. The
response was that access by the M grandparents was suspended immediately and
indefinitely.

[
49
]

At an earlier visit in October 2012, it was
reported that DM whispered to MJM, where MJM stated, “No, Abba [Hebrew for
father] hurt me”. MM then said to MJM, “God’s book tells us not to lie”. Ms.

A.        Facts

]

behalf), the Master gave oral reasons allowing the application for enforcement.
The formal order states that the thrice-amended Certificate of Review will be
entered as a judgment.

[
150
]

The appellant appealed from the Master to a
Queen’s Bench judge. After some delay in providing materials, an application by
the respondent to dismiss that appeal failed, and a judge ordered a hearing on
the merits. On September 6, 2013, a second judge heard argument from the appellant’s
husband. He also gave oral reasons, and dismissed the appeal.

[
151
]

The appellant now appeals from that chambers
judge to us.

B.        Grounds of Appeal

[
152
]

The three stated grounds of appeal in Part II of
the appellant’s factum are philosophical or vague, and brief. Our only
substantive comment on them is that Rules of Court are statutorily authorized
legislation, not optional guidelines. They bind courts and their officers, and
bind litigants.

[
153
]

Careful examination of the appellant’s factum
shows a considerable number of other more concrete topics argued or suggested. Some
crop up more than once in the factum.

[
154
]

We cannot discuss all of them, especially as
some palpably lack merit, or lack relevance at this stage of the proceedings. We
will try to give some prominence to those which seem to concern the appellant
the most.

[
155
]

It must be noted that the appellant does not
criticize the quality of Ms. Olszewski’s work. (The appellant does contend that
two procedural arrangements with the other side should have been referred to
the appellant for prior approval.)

C.        Discussion of Appellant’s Objections

1.         Who was Agreement With?

[
156
]

The appellant alleges that she hired only one
lawyer, Ms. Olszewski, Q.C., and not the respondent law firm. The lawyer was
obviously practising with and at the respondent law firm all the time. We doubt
very much that the appellant’s argument is sound in law.

[
157
]

In any event, it is pointless. If it were true,
it would lead only to clerical questions of form. It would be most unlikely to
affect what Ms. Olszewski does with the money when the bills are paid. If the
appellant wishes to make her cheque or money order payable to Ms. Olszewski,
that payee will suffice, and we much doubt that the respondent firm will mind.

[
158
]

A variant on that argument is the suggestion
that the review officer lacked jurisdiction because the firm, not the lawyer,
submitted the accounts for review. No authority for that is cited, and we know
of none. The majority of accounts submitted for taxation are probably by a law
firm of several lawyers, but for work done entirely, or largely, by one lawyer.
There is no question of jurisdiction. Must a law firm issue two appointments
for review, one in the name of the firm, and one in the name of the lawyer
doing the work? That would waste trees and ink, and benefit no one.

[
159
]

The lawyer in question swears that when she was hired
she said she would have a more junior (less expensive) lawyer assist her with
some work, in order to keep the bills down. That was very proper and wise. And
it does not sit well with the notion of a sole lawyer being hired.

2.         No Written Contract

[
160
]

It is elementary contracts law that a contract
may be made orally. Oral contracts are very rarely void, and most of them can
be enforced by either party. Written retainer agreements are now encouraged and
wise. But where the contract hiring a lawyer is not a contingency agreement
(and this one is not), no legislation or common-law rule requires writing. Indeed
there can be a valid implied contract to hire a lawyer and pay him or her. In
emergency situations, those are very common. On top of everything else, various
aspects of the arrangement here are evidenced, directly or indirectly, by
emails between the parties.

[
161
]

Therefore, the allegation that the respondent
misled the court by not telling the court that (allegedly) there was no
contract, has no foundation.

3.         Failure to Investigate the Facts?

[
162
]

In our court system, based on English law,
courts and their officers are basically passive, waiting for the parties to put
evidence and arguments to the court. That is modified a little when a lawyer’s
bill to his or her client is reviewed, but not a great deal. The review officer
usually acts properly when looking into what seem to be the issues argued by
the two sides, and not testing or starting an inquiry into, facts which seem to
have little relevance to those issues.

[
163
]

In this case, what the lawyer had done was not
obscure or unusual. Preparing for and arguing an appeal before the Court of
Appeal is a well-known procedure, and an experienced review officer would know
whether the time recorded, the type of work allegedly done, and the hourly rate
charged (or total fee) was unusually high or low. The review officer would not
have to reinvent the wheel.

[
164
]

In any event, we repeat that this is not an
appeal from the review officer, and the time for that passed over a year ago.

4.         Waiting for the Court of Appeal

[
165
]

The appellant complains that on the day of the
hearing before the Court of Appeal, her lawyers spent some hours waiting for
the Court before her appeal was heard. She thinks that the lawyers could have
done some other work for some other client while waiting.

[
166
]

At one time, the Court of Appeal gave no fixed
dates, and counsel would have to wait as much as three days, gowned, waiting to
be heard. Not being present when suddenly called invited loss by default of
appearance, or at least an irate Bench. Now the Court of Appeal usually fixes
appeals for a set day, but rarely is willing to fix a specific half day, still
less a precise hour. If (as usual) two appeals are set for the day, the Court
sets both for 10:00 a.m. Only then is any time estimate given. The Court will
sometimes tell counsel on the second appeal that they may leave for a set time
(rarely much more than an hour). That is all. If the first appeal is heard in a
fairly short time, then the wait is not long. But sometimes the first appeal
runs significantly longer than expected, indeed much longer than the times
estimated or the maximum time limits for oral argument fixed by the Practice
Directions. It is virtually impossible to predict that occurrence. Then
typically counsel on the second appeal are left waiting minute by minute
(except maybe for quite a brief luncheon break). Counsel have to be present,
gowned, and ready to argue.

[
167
]

Even with the aid of a computer or cell phone,
there is a limit to how much work a lawyer can do on other files during such a
wait. Going back to the lawyer’s office would consume most of the time
available, and be dangerous. Exceedingly few lawyers have (or can get) an
office within a block or two of the Law Courts in Edmonton.

[
168
]

Besides, arguing an appeal requires a lot of
physical, mental, and emotional preparation. A concert violinist waiting to go
on stage wisely does not help sweep the floors, nor do filing in the offices of
the symphony. Fighter pilots in 1940 waiting for the “scramble” call typically
could not relax enough even to read a magazine properly. Counsel are usually
too keyed up to do other work, and have their heads too full of the details of
the case at hand.

[
169
]

The appellant doubtless means no harm here, but
this objection is very unreasonable.

5.         Bias

[
170
]

The next topic is not so harmless. At some
length and more than once, the appellant contends that the chambers judge under
appeal was guilty of prejudgment and maybe other kinds of bias. This argument
greatly surprises us. We can see no trace of any such thing in the actions or
omissions of the judge, nor in any of his chosen language. The established
tests for appearance of bias to a reasonable informed bystander are not met
here, nor even approached.

[
171
]

Part of the problem is that the appellant
evidently does not understand the role of written argument in modern court
procedures. Written argument is often filed before the oral hearing (as was the
case here for what appears to have been a special application). Then the judge
is both permitted and expected to read it and master it. Forming some tentative
views is natural and proper, not a defect in character. Much more can be said
on even (say) 15 typed pages, than can be said in over an hour’s oral argument.
Oral argument is slow and inefficient. Not to mention the accuracy and lack of
need to take longhand notes, of written argument. It is perfectly proper for
the judge at the opening of oral argument to tell both sides where his or her
mind is then resting, or to suggest that one side initially need not argue, or
need not argue certain topics. That is why often more than one special
application is set for the same afternoon. Experienced counsel want such
guidance from the judge, and properly resent having to talk to a sphinx.

6.         Preferring the Client’s Word?

[
172
]

Another complaint is that the court must prefer
the client’s word to that of the lawyer, in a fee contest. There are some
chambers-level reported decisions from some other provinces which suggest
something of the sort. Even forgetting for the moment that this was not an
appeal from the review officer, we firmly disagree. (The appellant cites
Foco
v Strathcona Law Group
,
2011 ABQB 67
, 511 AR  148, but it appears to be
about ambiguity and interpretation of an agreement, not about fact disputes.)

[
173
]

The traditional oath of an English judge was to
try each case “without fear or favour”. The appellant forgets that she also
complains of bias. What if a judge said that any door-to-door salesman, or
politician, or used car dealer, would never be believed in that judge’s court
in the face of conflicting evidence? The judge then would be abandoning his or
her function. Is there any scientific evidence that lawyers almost always lie
about their fees, or have bad memories, and that clients are almost always
honest with a good memory? We doubt it. None was led here. It is especially odd
to apply such a rule to lawyers, who are subject to professional discipline, where
lying to a court would have obvious gravity.

7.         Use of Unexpected Authority

[
174
]

The appellant complains that she (or her
husband) was not expecting the counsel for the respondent firm to raise two
decided cases about the relevant limitation periods, during oral argument
before the chambers judge.

[
175
]

But her husband had just (briefly) raised the
limitations point in his oral argument (recorded on the preceding transcript page).
What did he expect the respondent’s counsel to do? Had counsel for the firm
raised a whole new unexpected issue, we might begin to see a point (though a
request for an adjournment or time to rebut would cure even that). But the appellant’s
agent raised the issue.

[
176
]

Besides, competent counsel must expect citation
of obvious authority on obvious points. The cases cited were not one hundred
years old, nor from Tasmania or West Virginia. It was the appellant’s idea for
herself and her husband to delve into these levels of appeal without much, if
any, professional legal assistance.

8.         Limitation Periods

[
177
]

Any idea that somehow the review of the accounts
was too late would have been for an appeal from review of the accounts, and
none was taken. Or indeed should have been raised earlier still. Limitation
periods do not oust court’s jurisdiction, and must be pleaded promptly.

9.         Was there a Ceiling?

[
178
]

The appellant alleges that the lawyer was told
that her bills could not exceed $35,000 because an insurer of the appellant had
imposed that ceiling (given policy limits). That point was made briefly by the
appellant’s husband to the Master and the chambers judge.

[
179
]

However, the lawyer’s affidavit denies (para 4)
that she was ever told to stop work when such a ceiling was reached. So this is
not a clear uncontradicted factual topic.

[
180
]

In any event, that is a matter well within the
jurisdiction of the review officer. If it was not raised before her, it is far
too late. If it was raised and ignored, then the appellant had a chance to
appeal the review and did not. And if it was raised and held against the
appellant, then there is no ground for complaint. We do not have a record of
what was told or not told to the review officer.

[
181
]

Further still, when it became very obvious that
the insurer considered the ceiling to have been met and would not cover an
account then outstanding, the law firm naturally refused to do more work
because the client was refusing to pay past bills. The appellant wanted more
work done, and so sent an email saying that she would personally pay the bills.
That is properly in evidence here, and was in evidence before the chambers
judge. More work was done (both for the Supreme Court anticipated proceedings,
and for finishing the work flowing from the Court of Appeal proceedings). Now
the appellant wants to go back on that deal.

10.       Was the Client the Insurance Company?

[
182
]

The appellant makes much of the fact that the
name on some of the accounts was the appellant’s insurance company, and that
some of the accounts were mailed to that company. She now hints (though does
not clearly state) that she had no personal liability to pay. That was very
briefly adverted to before the chambers judge, but not mentioned at all to the
Master. So the respondent had no chance to meet that with evidence.

[
183
]

There is nothing in the correspondence in
evidence to support such a view.

[
184
]

This argument clashes totally with the appellant’s
first argument, that she hired Ms. Olszewski personally. There is no suggestion
that the insurer sought out Ms. Olszewski, nor made any of the initial arrangements
with her. Nor is there any evidence or suggestion that the insurer had any
liability or exposure for any professional penalties. Yet the lawyer was hired
to appeal a serious professional discipline conviction (though not one of
dishonesty, we stress). An insurer cannot pay or indemnify removal from the
rolls, nor a suspension from practice. This was not a suit for damages.

[
185
]

There is no evidence of the terms of the
insurance policy, nor any suggestion that Ms. Olszewski was given it and told
to read it and conform to it.

[
186
]

And even if this had been a standard liability
policy, where the insurer would have to pay (indemnify) any liabilities
incurred if the defence failed, the law there is settled. Even if the insurer
picks and controls the defence lawyer, that lawyer is also acting for the
insured, who is also one of the clients. That has been repeatedly held by
Canadian and American courts in several contexts, especially the law of
insurance.

[
187
]

The appellant also complains of certain
decisions taken by the lawyer, and speaks of the appellant’s instructions to
the lawyer (again a matter for the review officer and a possible appeal from
her). But again that contradicts the appellant’s apparent suggestion here, that
the client was the insurance company, not the appellant.

[
188
]

The appellant seems to think she had what some
clients dream of, a retainer agreement in which all duties are owed to the
client, but no duties are owed by the client; especially not any obligation to
pay the lawyer. That is like a unicorn or a perpetual motion machine: no one
has found one yet.

[
189
]

In any event, even where there is a true
liability insurer with exposure, choosing and instructing counsel to defend a
suit against the insured, it has been held a number of times that the insured
has a contingent liability to pay the fees of the lawyer. And that is the basis
on which such counsel every day collect party-party costs when their insured
wins and the plaintiff loses. Rarely does the insured have to pay the lawyer’s
bills, but if the insurer for no good reason refused to pay, or became
insolvent, the insured would have to.

[
190
]

It is true that a review officer does not have
the power to decide contested questions about whether the lawyer has been
hired, or who is the client. But that does not mean that every decision by a
review officer is written in water, and can be set aside long after simply by
raising a late objection on such a topic. Rule 10.18 does not say that a review
officer’s decision cannot come to any final decision, and that is only about
amount. If that were so, then R 10.20 on enforcement of such a certificate
would be meaningless, and could never be used.

[
191
]

Rule 10.18 does not say that the review officer
cannot touch anything having to do with “the terms of a retainer agreement”. Instead,
R 10.18(1)(a) says that he or she “must refer any [such] question arising . . .
to the Court for a decision or direction.” “Question” must mean a dispute. That
dispute question must be known for the review officer to do that.

[
192
]

Someone appearing before an arbitrator or other
tribunal usually cannot keep silent about any known defect in jurisdiction, or
bias, and try to win on the merits, only raising the want of jurisdiction or
bias after he or she fails on the merits. Such conduct is not proper before a
review officer either.

[
193
]

One must note especially the substantive Rule
about reviews. Rule 10.19(4) and (5) say that the review officer must “certify
the amount to be paid by each party or person,” and that the certificate “. . .
is conclusive proof of the amount that a party or person who had notice of the
review must pay.”

[
194
]

If a review officer could not touch who is
liable to pay, then no certificate of review could comply with that Rule, and
none would ever have any final effect, nor ever be enforceable.

[
195
]

The Rules must be interpreted so that they fit
together, and none is futile.

D.        Conclusion

[
196
]

The other objections raised by the appellant
lack merit and do not justify prolonging the length of this judgment. We say as
much as we do, to give the lay appellant some explanation. We cannot turn this
judgment into an introductory text on the law of solicitors’ fees.

[
197
]

To the extent that any factual matters were in
issue, nothing before us even approaches palpable and overriding error. We cannot
upset the chambers judge.

[
198
]

The appeal is dismissed with costs.
